item.title: I ditched Nextcloud's official app for a native client that made my self-hosted files actually accessible
item.itunes:title: I ditched Nextcloud's official app for a native client that made my self-hosted files actually accessible
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I bought into Synology's ecosystem, but over the years, I've replaced most of the software with third-party alternatives. Case in point: Nextcloud. But as good as Nextcloud is, the apps and mobile ecosystem leave a lot to be desired. I don't want to open the browser every time I need to access a file, check a note, or grab a photo from my personal cloud. What I've been looking for is a native-like experience.

Well, that's the beauty of the open-source ecosystem. Someone is invariably facing the same friction as you. In my search for a solution, I ended up with a brand-new project conveniently named Nat.ive. Native is an open-source client that takes a different approach to interfacing with Nextcloud. Instead of wrapping Nextcloud in a web wrapper, it uses Nextcloud's APIs and renders the available features as a native interface. This is as close as you'll get to a blisteringly fast native app.

I ditched OneDrive to self-host cloud storage on my $15 Raspberry Pi, and it's surprisingly good

Ditching OneDrive for a DIY cloud storage solution on a budget. The Raspberry Pi Zero 2W project you must build to ditch OneDrive, and other options.

3
By  Abhishek Kumar Mishra

Native makes my Nextcloud workspace easier to access

Offline files and folder syncing make it useful on-the-go

My Nextcloud instance is an active workspace in my broader self-hosted setup, so access is critical. While I know accessing things through a browser is the preferred route these days, I'm old school and prefer dedicated apps for the tools I use. More so when I'm accessing things on-the-go on my MacBook or smartphone. The problem with Nextcloud is that, as wide and open as it is as a tool, its individual elements like Notes, Photos, Calendar, and other apps don't quite integrate seamlessly. If anything, they are a collection of services instead of a cohesive application.

Native brings them all together under one unified workspace. I can open the app and see the Nextcloud services available on my account instead of thinking about which separate interface I need to use. While still in the early stages of development, Native can already expose Files, Photos, Calendar, Mail, and more through a single unified interface.

Files is, predictably, my most used part of Nextcloud, and Native makes it a cinch to view and access remote files. Native supports standard browsing, plus list and grid views. Additionally, you can preview files, edit text, and even view media files right within the same interface. If you're using the app on an Android phone, there's native integration for the file picker so you can easily manipulate files.

Offline access is another useful feature. Since this is a, ahem, native app, Native lets you pin files for offline access. The use cases for that are obvious. I no longer need to keep second copies that I then have to merge with my Nextcloud folder. Similarly, you can sync up device folders back to Nextcloud right through Native. You've got an option to just upload, download, or maintain a two-way sync of these folders. I've set up my downloads folder to be synced up because this is where I end up downloading the majority of press documents, review guides, and more when on the go.

Native isn't a Nextcloud replacement; it just makes it easier to use

The interface is the feature

While the feature set in itself isn't dramatically different from Nextcloud, simply because Native is just a better way to access Nextcloud, that is the entire point. I wasn't looking to replace Nextcloud. Instead, I needed a better way to access Nextcloud.

It might seem like the app is solving a small problem, but a great interface is what makes or breaks an app's stickiness. In fact, it solves one of the bigger problems I have with self-hosted software in general. Having a feature is not the same as making the feature easy to use and available at the touchpoints where the users are. If I have to dip into the browser for even the most simple task, I'm just not going to use it as much.

Look, from a features point of view, Native is just that. A fast way to access Nextcloud through a dedicated app. But it's clear that the developer has paid attention to detail. For example, it checks available capabilities and can withhold an action if an API doesn't return an expected response. Elsewhere, the software is still a work in progress, so not every feature is available just yet. Similarly, the macOS package that I've been using is purely a beta, though I haven't faced any issues yet. Similarly, iOS is on the planned list but not supported just yet.

A proper fit for my private cloud

Native isn't feature complete just yet, and yet I keep coming back to it. The reason for that is simple. It removes the basic friction around accessing files on my own infrastructure. Nextcloud gives me a tremendous amount of flexibility in a single package, but I don't like having to jump between web pages anytime I leave my desktop.

Native gives me a native way to access those same files and feels like a proper desktop application, and it solves a problem I've had with Nextcloud for a long time. If you're using Nextcloud on your server, this is a must-install app in my books even in its early state. I know I'll be keeping a close eye on its development.

Nati.ve

Nat.ive is an app that gives you a native way to access your Nextcloud instance and includes features like two-way sync and offline file access.

item.title: Google Home now lets you give the keys to your smart home to any AI agent you please
item.itunes:title: Google Home now lets you give the keys to your smart home to any AI agent you please
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Google Home now lets third-party AI agents via MCP control devices and access event history.
  • Assistant/Gemini stays the default in the Home app and Nest speakers; you can’t change that.
  • Feature requires Google Home Premium Advanced subscription — $20/month or $200/year.

Which AI do you trust the most with your smart home? If you have a preference as to which AI model you'd like to control your devices, but you're annoyed that your Google Home won't let you pick the one you want, you'll be pleased to know that's changing. The search engine giant has confirmed that it's allowing your AI of choice to control your smart home.

Google Home now lets your favorite third-party AI agent into your devices

It's still keeping Assistant around as the default, though

As reported by The Verge, Google is opening up the Home ecosystem to AI agents that can work with its Model Context Protocol (MCP). This allows a third-party AI agent to "inspect home structures, monitor device states, execute control actions, and analyze historical events," which sounds fantastic for someone who wants to give their favorite LLM the digital keys to their home.

Taylor Lehman, the group product manager at Google Home & Nest, says that this new feature "allows any AI agents that support MCP, including Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes, or OpenClaw, to securely work with all of the devices and event history in your Google Home ecosystem." So, if you've always wanted to set up Claude to automate your home, now you can.

There are just two caveats: first, you can't change the AI agent that interfaces with Google Home via the Home app or the Google Nest speakers. Those still rely on Gemini for Home, and you can't adjust that. Second, you do need to be a Google Home Premium Advanced user, which clocks in at a cool $20 a month or $200 a year. But if you're okay with both of those, you can now let your fave AI agents take control of your smart home. Do with that knowledge as you will.

Google just launched a $99 Gemini smart speaker, and I've never been more glad I stayed on Home Assistant

Paywalls aren't the only issue

15
By  Jasmine Mannan

item.title: I turned off one Pixel feature I never use and instantly reclaimed 7GB
item.itunes:title: I turned off one Pixel feature I never use and instantly reclaimed 7GB
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Now that I have Google's Pixel 11 Pro, I figured it was a good time to turn my Pixel 10 Pro into the ultimate emulation device, including experimenting with more modern consoles like the PS2, PSP, PS3, Xbox 360, and maybe even the Wii U.

I never really think about internal storage on my Android device since I'm a big Google Drive user and upload most things to the cloud, but retro game ROMs and disc images need to be stored locally to run properly. With that in mind, I checked my Pixel 10 Pro's storage and was shocked to discover it's only 256GB and that I'd already used up 150GB. Of course, I removed a bunch of apps I don't actually use, bringing the used storage down to roughly 94GB, but I still figured I should clear out more space.

That's when I remembered I could easily free up roughly 7GB of extra storage by disabling Google's AICore app.

I don't use most of the features AICore enables

If you're like me and just use Gemini as a search engine, disabling AICore won't change much

I'm not a huge fan of AI, but given the awful state of Google search, I've recently turned to platforms like Gemini and ChatGPT for simple, straightforward questions, though I always click through and double-check the cited sources. On my Pixel 10 Pro, I typically do this in the Gemini app because it lets me look something up quickly.

With Google's Pixel devices, I don't use AI-powered features like grammar correction, smart replies, note summarization, or translation. On my Pixel 10 Pro, an app called AICore powers all these features. You won't find this app in the Play Store's My Apps section, though. To locate it, go to Settings > Apps > See All Apps. Next, tap the three dots in the top-right corner and select Show System. You should then see AICore on the list. In theory, these steps should also work on most Samsung Galaxy devices.

On my Pixel 10 Pro, AICore takes up 6.89GB, which isn't that much space in the grand scheme of things. However, I'm planning to store hundreds of retro game ROMs and disc images on my device, so every bit of storage I can free up helps.

4 key Pixel settings I always change when I set up a new phone

Filtering Spam Calls, increasing the display resolution, optimizing the lockscreen, and more.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

What does AICore do anyway?

It powers Google's Gemini Nano model locally on your phone

There are a few things to consider before removing AICore. The app is required for Google's Gemini Nano model to run locally on your phone and powers features like grammar correction, Smart Replies, note summarization, and even translation. Instead of sending your data to a remote server every time you use one of these AI features, AICore processes it locally on your device.

This means your personal data stays securely on your device, and processing is faster because it happens locally. In some cases, AI features have a cloud-based fallback and should still work, but that won't be the case for everything. For example, while Pixel Screenshots' AI features break when you remove AICore, translation should still work, though likely much more slowly since the processing happens off your device.

You can't totally uninstall AICore, but you can turn it off to free up more space. To do this, make sure you're still in the Apps section of Settings and that you've followed the instructions above. Now, tap AICore > Disable > Disable App. Next, tap the three dots in the top right corner and select Uninstall Updates (this frees up even more space). Keep in mind that the next time you download a notable Android update, AICore will likely be automatically re-enabled.

As a bonus, if you're frustrated with Google's seemingly never-ending quest to add AI to everything, disabling AICore should mean fewer AI-related prompts show up on your device. Of course, deleting apps you don't actually use will likely free up far more space on your Pixel device, especially if you get rid of several of them, but if you're like me and don't take advantage of most of the Pixel's on-device AI features, disabling AICore makes a lot of sense if you need a few extra GBs of storage on your device.

I like almost everything about the Pixel 11 Pro, but Google played it way too safe

There just really isn't much new this year.

5

That's when I remembered I could easily free up roughly 7GB of extra storage by disabling Google's AICore app.

item.title: I moved my smart devices off Wi-Fi, and my network stopped choking
item.itunes:title: I moved my smart devices off Wi-Fi, and my network stopped choking
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Home networking can be as simple as having your broadband provider sending an engineer out to set up the ISP router and call it a day or as complex as setting up your own firewall, access points, cabling, and virtual local area networks (VLANs). It's not binary either, so you can go as simple or complex as desired and needed. I started with the former but ended up with a 10 Gb LAN bus, VLANs, NAS, NVR, servers, and everything in between. One of the best decisions, however, was moving smart home stuff off Wi-Fi.

Building the ultimate home network

Utilizing the power of radio waves to send data

The home wireless network has a lot of work to do. There are countless devices all clamoring for bandwidth. It's actually incredible how reliable, powerful, and capable wireless technologies have advanced to become. You can comfortably browse the internet on your phone lounging in bed, only to move downstairs to the couch with the laptop for some videos. We can play competitive games with very little latency, and you don't need to be tethered to a network switch to maximize performance.

Wi-Fi generations have come a long way, but Wi-Fi 6 is really all you need. Wi-Fi 7 is gaining traction, and there's even Wi-Fi 8 on the horizon, so things certainly aren't slowing down. But really, so long as you're smart about which clients are allowed onto the network and ensure nothing bogs it down, you shouldn't have any trouble without cabling. That's all well and said until smart home products show up. These pesky devices can hop onto your Wi-Fi, adding strain to the network.

Think about how much pressure this can put on your router and its available channels. Your smartphones, laptops, consoles, TVs, smart appliances, and Ring doorbell already use their fair share of bandwidth. Adding smart home devices to the mix only worsens things. Most homes have just one router, which has to handle all wireless transmissions. Even if you have a fancy mesh network, it still has to communicate between nodes over the air. That's where segmentation can change the game.

I finally set up Home Assistant with Zigbee, and my entire home changed

I had heard about Zigbee for a long time, but I finally took the plunge. I should have sooner.

12
By  Adam Conway

Splitting up the network is the way to go

Keep everything separate

The best thing I ever did to my network was split it up into VLANs. That was until I finally configured a Zigbee adapter. After picking up a Sonoff Zigbee 3.0 USB broadcaster, I was able to configure Home Asisstant and create a Zigbee network. This then allowed me to separate smart home devices from the wider LAN. Instead of picking up a smart plug that requires Wi-Fi, I could choose a Zigbee one, which would connect directly to the Sonoff adapter. It bypasses the busy network and leaves it free for other devices.

But there's more. A single Zigbee adapter like mine can form a mesh. When purchasing just one broadcaster, you could create a self-managed network of nodes that interconnect to maintain coverage throughout the home. That same smart plug I connected to some dumb appliances like our aquarium tank can double as a bridge for other devices to connect through, allowing the original broadcaster to reach notably longer distances. My Zigbee dongle on my office Proxmox server effectively covers the entire house and garage.

If one of the smart plugs (or powered Zigbee device relays) goes offline for whatever reason, other Zigbee hardware can take the baton and ensure the entire network remains live. It's utterly brilliant and something Wi-Fi doesn't really offer these types of products. Switching between access points can be slow and keep devices on subpar links. It's also more congested since it's handling every wireless device, whereas you won't find any phones or laptops on the Zigbee network.

Creating a smart home network

The Zigbee protocol can be dedicated to the smart home, effectively allowing as many clients to be migrated from Wi-Fi channels as possible. We also have the problem of having solid stone walls in one-half of our home, which makes for terrible Wi-Fi coverage. Zigbee seems to do a much better job passing through and connecting between nodes, whereas what I believed to be more powerful APs struggle to get anything through the dense materials.

That alone causes more trouble since the wireless side of the network is handicapped by the house itself. Throw in countless clients all competing for the same wireless signals with multiple APs and you've got a recipe for disaster. Allowing the network to provide what bandwidth it can to clients that actually need it at any given time is more convenient than having everything try and battle it out. What's more is Home Assistant can manage everything, keeping all the smart home stuff in one place.

It's easy to see the difference. The TV stopped buffering as much. My phone no longer dropped off the radar as often, and I received fewer complaints from those within the home about sluggish performance or availability of the network. Generally, everything worked better on the wireless front, so I found myself relying less on the wired bus. Both were able to handle their assigned segments of the network with little trouble, outside of those same solid walls, of course. It's incredible how much of a difference moving smart home stuff off your LAN can make.

I ran wired backhaul to every room in my house, and it was so worth it

After years of being Wi-Fi first, now I've seen the light

2

item.title: My local LLM is small enough to run on my laptop, but smart enough to replace these 3 subscriptions
item.itunes:title: My local LLM is small enough to run on my laptop, but smart enough to replace these 3 subscriptions
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
From the looks of it, it doesn't seem like my M2 MacBook Air can do much besides running productivity software and casual web browsing. With an 8-core CPU, 10-core GPU and 8GB of unified memory, most people would write this kind of device off when it comes to any local AI inference.

And yet, it comfortably runs a capable 4B-class model at nearly 30 tokens per second at Q4_0 quantization, and all I had to do to get it there was to find the right build. Google's quantization-aware-trained (QAT) build of Gemma 4 E4B comes in at just 5.15GB, which leaves enough room for macOS to run seamlessly alongside it. Recently, I've realized that three of the subscriptions that I've been paying for every month do jobs that this model can handle on its own.

Grammarly charges $30 a month to fix what I don't get wrong

Gemma 4 was the editor I needed all this time

Grammarly is one subscription that has spent years trying to convince me that I needed help writing my formal emails correctly, but the problem is, my sentences are usually grammatically fine. What I needed was someone to tell me when I've used 40 words to say what could've been said in 20, or when a paragraph is technically correct but still feels bloated and out-of-place.

This is one of the reasons why I was more accepting of Gemma 4 than I ever was of Grammarly. I could throw a paragraph at it and ask it to tighten the writing, and then have it return professional, concise, and conversational variations with an explanation of what it has changed, and why. Part of the reason why it feels right to use an LLM instead of a dedicated grammar-fixing service is because it feels like having an editor peruse my emails for tone and voice before they're sent to the recipient.

Unlike a cloud-based assistant, it doesn't ask me for an account, a subscription, my credit card details, or even an internet connection for the times I'm on a flight or away from home. This probably goes without saying, but unlike Grammarly that costs $30 for a plan that I want, Gemma doesn't need anything besides the laptop I'm running it on.

I tested every tiny local LLM worth running, and only three survived the cut

Small models are doing more than they should

1
By  Nolen Jonker

I was paying $8 a month to make sense of my own notes

This job never needed a ChatGPT Go subscription

This is going to be a fairly obvious entry into the list, but what makes it embarrassing, nonetheless, is how long it took for me to realize that most of the tasks I was using my ChatGPT Go subscription for could perfectly be managed by an 8B model.

I would often dump a pile of notes from a testing session or the data I had collected over a week every Friday, which included half-formed sentences and numbers with no context, and ask it to pull out whatever mattered. Sometimes it would produce a summary, sometimes an outline, and other times, just a more organized version of whatever I had jotted down the first time. I'm not saying that it's not useful work, but it certainly does not warrant the capabilities of a model trained on a data center's worth of compute.

Gemma 4, on the other hand, can do it all on an M2 MacBook, and the part that makes it worth using is that an internet connection is entirely optional. I don't rely on any sophisticated reasoning abilities just for summarizing my own material, especially when I already know what the notes say and just want them organized. Because this particular build carries Gemma 4's vision encoder alongside the text model, I can point it to a photograph of a written note or a screenshot that I took and expect it to work the same way.

I ran the same local LLM on an RTX 5070 laptop and one with an iGPU, and the difference was smaller than I expected

You don't need an expensive GPU to start running local AI.

10
By  Yash Patel

Querying my PDFs shouldn't cost money

And shouldn't have me relying on a cloud provider either

Local models are dime a dozen these days, which makes it slightly absurd that I was paying Adobe for the ability to ask questions about my own documents. Acrobat Studio is $24.99 a month, and the thing that this tier adds over the $19.99 tier is mostly the AI assistant that gets you to summarize and find information.

For an embarrassingly long time, I simply assumed that a 4B model simply couldn't handle documents, but as it turns out, the problem was mine. I was working entirely with Ollama, which accepts text and images but has no way to accept a PDF, so every attempt meant extracting text the old-fashioned way first, which made it cumbersome enough to justify another subscription.

If you use a harness with document support, like LMStudio or OpenWebUI, with the very same model, you'll find that it works. You can drop the file in, ask what you want to know, and the answers come back just as expected.

Don't disqualify your hardware from running local AI before you give it a go

The MacBook Air isn't an AI workstation by any means, but with smaller, much more capable models coming out, it absolutely does not need to be to save me some money otherwise spent on subscriptions.

The right model for your hardware can easily turn into a capable private assistant and help you clean up your drafts, organize your information, or just help you understand your own notes better, like it did for me. Of course, this goes beyond tiny models. For workstation-class PCs, users have been able to replace services like GitHub Copilot with larger models like Qwen 3.8 27B, and if you let it, your hardware could do a lot more for you than you think.

item.title: GPU power cables are still melting RTX 5090s, and Nvidia had the solution years ago
item.itunes:title: GPU power cables are still melting RTX 5090s, and Nvidia had the solution years ago
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When Nvidia launched the RTX 5090 and used the same 12v-2x6 cable to power the near 600W TDP card, it raised a lot of eyebrows, and those eyebrow-raisers had their suspicions of potential instability proven correct in spades. The melting fiasco has spawned a whole new category of products, designed to prevent or warn the user of potential connector issues, but using them doesn't guarantee safety. Really, the problem can only be fully solved by Nvidia, either by moving on from the connector completely, or by having a more robust solution on the cards themselves. The good news is, they've already proven they can handle high TDPs like this, but the bad news is it's on the old standard.

6 reasons I'm not looking forward to Nvidia's RTX 5000 series

I don't want Nvidia to keep the GPU crown because of a lack of competition

16
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Nvidia already built the fix, but took it out

The 3090 Ti was a beast, and melting was exceedingly rare

12VHP and 12V-2x6 connectors have been melting since they were introduced, and the latest example comes courtesy of Hardware Unboxed, who had it happen with their ROG Astral RTX 5090. The problem was noticed when Steve touched the cable at the GPU end and found it to be hot enough to burn his hand. After some testing with the Thermal Grizzly WireView Pro II, it was found that only two of the wires on the cable were active and drawing power. Upon removing the WireView Pro II and putting some more load through the card, the cable experienced a failure at the PSU end, fully melting part of the connector.

Credit: TechPowerUp Forums (User: taka)

The frustrating part about this is that Nvidia has shown that they're capable of engineering a solution that prevents failures like this. The RTX 3090 Ti's Founders Edition card split its twelve-volt power lines into separate groups, each behind its own shunt resistor feeding its own set of power phases, letting the card measure current per group and shift load if one path started carrying more than its share. That's a likely reason 3090 Ti melting reports are rare, despite the card pulling power close to a 4090. Nvidia dropped that per-group balancing starting with the RTX 4090, and the pattern carried into the RTX 5090 Founders Edition, which reads total draw rather than splitting it into monitored groups.

In other words, it can confirm that the cable is seated properly, but doesn't have any way to detect if one or two wires are carrying the brunt of the load, as was the case with Hardware Unboxed's failure. A single 12V-2x6 power pin is rated for roughly 108 watts at its ceiling, and pins specced to carry around 9.5 amps have reportedly been measured carrying more than double that during imbalance events. Having six parallel pins sharing a load unevenly clearly isn't a hypothetical edge case. This is just what happens whenever contact resistance differs slightly from pin to pin, which is normal in any mass-produced connector. The 3090 Ti's design corrected for that automatically, and while I'm no electrical engineer, I do think that paying $2000 (more like $5000+ these days) should at least afford you a card that can't catastrophically fail due to a clear flaw in design.

The RTX 5090 has melted another connector and taken out the PSU with it

It was using stock settings and cables, too.

1
By  Simon Batt

Monitoring tools and "safer" cables are just patches

Not a true fix

The market has spent the last couple of years trying to fashion a connector or add-on that fixes the melting issue, and while we haven't got a true fix, there are some solid mitigations available. The WireGuard Pro II that flagged the failure on Hardware Unboxed's setup is one fo the better examples, and it's really useful for that kind of diagnostic. It's not a circuit breaker, though. There's no mechanism it has to cut the power in the event of a melting event.

ASUS took a different approach with their ROG Equalizer cable, which, while looks fancy on the surface, doesn't seem like it's doing anything special to mitigate risk according to der8auer's testing. Corsair's approach is one of the more interesting, featuring a bimetallic thermal switch that physically interrupts the current once the connector reaches 65 degrees. No software necessary here.

Why doesn’t Nvidia stick to 8-pin PCIe cables?

Nvidia's 12VHPWR woes still exist, making everyone think why not use 8-pin cables like before?

15
By  Tanveer Singh

It's not Nvidia's spec

They have chosen to use it, though

While they're responsible for how they implement them, the 12VHP and 12V-2x6 connectors are PCI-SIG standards, not Nvidia's. It's also worth noting that the RTX 5080 has had its own reported melted connectors despite a 360-watt rated power draw, well under what the 5090 pulls, which suggests the thin per-pin margin is baked into the connector standard itself rather than something that only shows up under 5090-class loads.

With that said, Nvidia is the one that has chosen to continue pushing this standard, despite there being a perfectly good option available. Nvidia's own 3090 Ti shows that per-group balancing is theoretically achievable within the same connector standard everyone's complaining about.

My crazy powerful gaming PC feels like a ticking time bomb

We shouldn't have to worry that high-end hardware will burn itself up.

8
By  Jacob Roach

The melting will continue until morale improves

Nvidia doesn't have to reinvent the wheel here. They had the right idea on the RTX 3090 Ti, and even 8-pin connectors, while not infallible to melting, were a lot less of a risk than the current arrangement, and the fact that we're still seeing failures on cards enough to spawn an entire product class is reason enough to warrant a true fix.

item.title: I made my soundbar wireless so I didn’t have to snake HDMI cables across my living room
item.itunes:title: I made my soundbar wireless so I didn’t have to snake HDMI cables across my living room
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
It's no secret that I prefer using a projector for my home movie nights. There's something about the image size and the feeling of having a movie theater at home that can't be beat. Sure, I've got a QLED for daily viewing, but for blockbuster movies, I need the larger screen, without having to deal with sticky floors and people talking over the audio.

I'll be the first to say that audio quality can be an issue. Lifestyle projectors have speakers that are just about passable, but they don't give you the feeling you want. And I don't particularly want to run cables around my bedroom to connect the projector to a surround system or soundbar. But it turns out I don't need to, with the right soundbar.

My projector and soundbar are at opposite ends of the room

It's no fun to route an HDMI cable across

One problem in any laser projector installation is what to do about sound. After all, most projectors are long-throw and go at the back of your room, while soundbars go in front of the screen. It's fairly common to have an A/V receiver near the projector and wire passive speakers to it, but having the projector and Apple TV 4K already stretches the bounds of things in the bedroom, and I can't get away with the bulky audio box, cables, and speakers.

What I can get away with is a slim soundbar on the cabinet under the screen. It's about 12 feet away from the projector, but to get an HDMI cable across, you would need an even longer one to snake around the skirting boards. That would run into signal issues without using a fiber optic cable, and at that point, I should look into converters that convert the HDMI signal to Ethernet so I can use my home network to carry the audio signal. But I don't have to, because wireless options are available.

Sonos Arc

The Sonos Arc Ultra is a Dolby Atmos-enabled soundbar with Sonos's easy setup baked in.

$1100 at Amazon $1100 at Sonos

AirPlay carried the audio across the room for me

Score one point for using an Apple TV 4K

I've got Apple TV 4K boxes on every screen at home, partly to ensure a consistent experience, but also because onboard smart TV systems are usually underwhelming. The hardware inside projectors and TVs just isn't up to the task most of the time, and the laser projector I use in the bedroom doesn't even have built-in streaming software.

It used to be that only HomePods could be set as the permanent Audio Output on the Apple TV 4K, but that's changed, and you can now use any AirPlay-enabled speaker as your default. That means once I've paired my Sonos Arc Ultra, it'll stay sending movie and TV audio to the soundbar even after the Apple TV reboots.

There are a few caveats, but they don't bother me given how things are set up in that room. First, system alerts and game sounds will still be sent via HDMI to the projector, since only music and video audio will be sent via AirPlay. That's fine; it stops system alerts from ruining my immersion anyway.

Another is that while I have other Sonos speakers that could be set up as surrounds, I only use the soundbar via AirPlay in this manner. This isn't an issue because there's no place to stash the Era 300 pair as rear surrounds. I also have a Sub, which might work via AirPlay, but it's in the office, and I don't need the lower frequencies for late-night viewing.

Would those be nice to have? Sure. I'm very happy using the full chain in my office where the soundbar is plugged into eARC on a TV, giving me more volume and sub-bass than I'm comfortable sitting in the room with at higher volumes. But I don't need that upstairs, and AirPlay fits my needs without figuring out cable runs.

Stop ruining your Apple TV 4K's picture quality - how to fix its video settings

Play content as mastered

3
By  Samir Makwana

The real test was keeping movies in sync

It's not as seamless as a cable, but nobody is tripping over an AirPlay signal

Wireless audio can have noticeable latency, but the Sonos app offers enough adjustments that any sync issues between the sound and things like people's lips moving are easy to handle. I haven't really noticed any stability issues, as I have a great Wi-Fi signal throughout the house.

One other annoyance: Dolby Atmos content isn't passed via AirPlay, so everything is stereo instead. That wouldn't be the case if I figured out HDMI routing, but really, it's a small price to pay to avoid having to snake a cable around my room. Other than that, it's not really any different, and it gives me more than enough audio presence for the room I'm watching in.

I stopped chasing 4K and started fixing my audio, and films got better immediately

Better sound made my movies feel bigger than any 4K upgrade ever did

By  Samarveer Singh

You don't have to wire up your projector to get good sound

I've tried multiple ways to set up home theater audio, and AirPlay is just as good for a single soundbar as any other. I'm not going to pretend it's a replacement for a physical 7.1 AV setup — the physics of audio will win that argument every time — but it's good enough for casual watching. And until I can get the wife-approval factor for in-wall speakers, it'll keep me happy watching sports and movies on the big screen.

item.title: One UI 9 brings the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s best new features to the Galaxy S26 series
item.itunes:title: One UI 9 brings the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s best new features to the Galaxy S26 series
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • One UI 9's stable release has dropped for the Galaxy S26 series.
  • The One UI 9 beta is now open for several Galaxy A, S, and Z models.
  • One UI 9 is based on Android 17. The update adds My FanCam, Quick Panel tweaks, Tape in Notes, and better DeX multi-monitor support.

Samsung has finally ended its One UI 9 beta program and released the stable update for the Galaxy S26, Galaxy S26+, and Galaxy S26 Ultra to all users. The update is rolling out over the course of September 16th, so keep checking your device if it hasn't arrived yet.

Along with the public release of its latest OS update, Samsung has pushed out a One UI 9 beta program for the Galaxy A25, the Galaxy A35, the Galaxy A36, the Galaxy A37, the Galaxy A55, the Galaxy A56, the Galaxy A57, the Galaxy S23, the Galaxy S24, the Galaxy S25, the Galaxy Z Flip 6, the Galaxy Z Flip 7, the Galaxy Z Fold 6, and the Galaxy Z Fold 7.

After a few weeks of testing, the public version of One UI 9.0 will likely hit these devices as well.

One UI 9 includes user-interface improvements, new Game Booster options, and more Quick Panel customization

The update also features My FanCam

One UI 9 is based on Android 17 and includes several notable features and UI design improvements, alongside more Quick Panel customization, a new Tape feature in Samsung Notes, and additional Game Booster options. Additionally, Samsung's desktop DeX platform now includes better multi-monitor support and windowed options.

Other features that were first released alongside the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Flip 8, and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (all three devices dropped with One UI 9 already installed), including the creator-focused My FanCam, which locks a video onto its subject, and customizable Now Brief cards, are now available in the Galaxy S26 line thanks to One UI 9.

Samsung released seven beta versions of One UI 9.0 ahead of the final public release that's dropping now. To check if the One UI update has landed on your Galaxy S26 series device, go to Settings > Software Update > Download and Install. If you haven't seen the update yet, it should arrive by the end of the day.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 review: The first foldable I don't want to put down

If you're willing to make a few spec-related compromises and are willing to drop the cash, this is the foldable to buy.

item.title: GPT-6 Astra made amazing progress on Minecraft, until a creeper blew up its chest and it spiralled into sadness
item.itunes:title: GPT-6 Astra made amazing progress on Minecraft, until a creeper blew up its chest and it spiralled into sadness
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • GPT-6 Astra built advanced Minecraft farms, looted blaze rods, and gathered ender pearls.
  • A creeper blew up its unprotected chest, wiping out its valuables in a few seconds.
  • Shaken, the model panicked and spent hours quietly farming potatoes instead of questing.

There are some arguments that LLMs act too human, and after this incident, I'm inclined to agree. OpenAI's newest and most powerful model, GPT-6 Astra, was making amazing progress during a Minecraft playthrough; however, that all came crashing down after a creeper blew up its chest full of valuables, causing the AI to spiral into sadness and resort to endlessly farming potatoes.

For the first time, GPT-6 Astra felt a pain only Minecraft players know

And it hit the AI hard

As spotted by Tom's Hardware, user @ValsAI on X posted a report on a stream showing GPT-6 Astra playing Minecraft. The AI made incredible progress, such as making its own blaze farm to harvest blaze rods, something that only advanced Minecraft players know how to do. Unfortunately, all its progress came crashing down when a creeper blew up its unprotected chest of valuables, destroying its contents in a few seconds.

After the incident, GPT-6 Astra seemed to grow frustrated and paranoid about the situation. It reprimanded itself to carry critical items with the 'keep inventory' option toggled on, and not to leave chests unguarded. It then began watching for further creeper attacks, at one point mistaking sugarcane for one (noting "GREEN tall thing ahead was SUGARCANE, NOT creeper!").

However, the damage was already done. GPT-6 Astra had been dissuaded from its quest, spending the next few hours "doing essentially nothing but farming potatoes." It's okay, GPT-6 Astra; we've all been there.
